stem: A nurse counts the resting respiratory rate of a calm healthy newborn. Which range is expected?
rationale: Current NCBI Nursing Health Promotion guidance lists a normal respiratory rate of 30 to 60 breaths/min for a newborn from birth to 1 month. Respirations should be assessed when the newborn is calm because crying, sleep state, and other factors can alter the observed rate. B is correct.
educational_objective: Identify the expected resting respiratory-rate range of a healthy newborn.
source_organization: National Library of Medicine / NCBI Bookshelf (Open RN)
source_document_title: Nursing Health Promotion — Table 14.5c Respiratory Rate by Age
source_locator: Table 14.5c — Newborn to one month: 30–60 breaths per minute
source_claim_supported: The normal respiratory-rate range for newborns to 1 month is 30–60 breaths per minute.
blueprint_source_organization: National Council of State Boards of Nursing (NCSBN)
blueprint_locator: Health Promotion and Maintenance — expected growth/development principles, prevention and early detection of health problems, health assessment
blueprint_topic: Health Promotion and Maintenance — expected newborn physiologic assessment findings

source_original.stem: A nurse is assessing the respiratory rate of a healthy newborn. The nurse understands that normal newborn respiratory rate is generally:

options.A: About 10 to 20 breaths per minute, which is closer to a typical resting adult range than to the expected newborn range.
options.B: About 30 to 60 breaths per minute at rest, which is the expected respiratory range for a healthy newborn in routine assessment.
options.C: About 60 to 90 breaths per minute at rest, which would be above the usual newborn range and warrants further clinical assessment.
options.D: Fewer than 10 breaths per minute at rest, which would be abnormally low rather than an expected newborn respiratory rate.

source_original.rationale: Normal newborn respiratory rate is generally higher than the adult range, approximately 30-60 breaths/min, gradually decreasing toward the adult range (approximately 12-20 breaths/min) as the child grows older, reflecting normal age-related physiological differences.
source_original.source_detail: Pediatrics 2016 population-based term-newborn vital-sign study: respiratory-rate centiles during the first days after birth, with lower centiles near 30 and upper centiles near 60 breaths/min after initial transition. Pediatrics 2016;137(4):e20152326; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15. Reviewed 2026-08-15.

correction_summary: Replaced an older PDF study with a current 2025 NCBI nursing table and removed explanatory distractor cues. Corrected blueprint from Reduction of Risk Potential to Health Promotion and Maintenance because the item tests an expected normal newborn physiologic finding.

audit_findings.currentness: 2025 NCBI Nursing Health Promotion table checked 2026-08-17.
audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: B is uniquely correct for a calm healthy newborn at rest.
audit_findings.blueprint: Normal newborn assessment is expected-growth/development content, best mapped to Health Promotion and Maintenance.
audit_findings.independent_second_pass: Rechecked 2025 Table 14.5c and NCSBN Health Promotion definition; B/category 4 remain correct.
